title: Max Roach's nobility, rejection of 'jazz', and the Beijing Trio
summary: Jang portrays Max Roach as noble and collective-minded, covering Sid Catlett, the Beijing Trio name and the SenseUs anthem project.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: What did Max Roach have that was unique? What was unique about Max Roach?

He was very noble. I remember when we performed Duke Ellington’s “Come Sunday” I could see the humble and humility. And I mean he was a real warrior and you know, some of the works I pay tribute some of the great artists, like Paul Robeson and Mei Manfang. You know I’m trying to respect those artists who’ve become forgotten. Or like I would say one day American — or one day great American artists and one day alien, with a persecution, and the unofficial ban on Paul Robeson’s life during the McCarthy period of the 1950’s, but he’s one of the greatest American artists. And so I pay tribute to him. When Max Roach, when I saw him perform with Sid Catlett on the hi-hat, see there’s that stickiness, that personality. What he does on the hi-hat, a solo piece, and then it brings your attention to who was Sid Catlett? I mean I’m finding — there may be students here that don’t know who Max Roach is. So now I’ve been thinking about, well God, there’s so many legacies I feel — I don’t know if I have to say protect, or if I have to try to preserve. And then there’s my own legacy. Because it’s been — but then now I have to accept that I have no control over that. Now Max, when I was working with him, he rejected the term jazz. In fact, one of the working titles of his book that he working on Max was “Jazz is a Four Letter Word.” Because his reference is to fornication. You know it came out of the New Orleans bordellos. Louis Armstrong hated New Orleans, although he said that Louis Armstrong was the most political person because he saw Louis Armstrong’s face, a smiling face, and then he saw the weariness and sorrow in a hotel room. So he saw the power and sorrow of Louis Armstrong. You know Max Roach, I mean he was a person of integrity. When we recorded the Beijing Trio he — well for me, I thought okay let’s call it the Max Roach Jon Jang Duo. You know, have his name first, this way we could attract more listeners, sell more CD’s. But he really believed in the collective. You know this music is about democracy. And he wanted to call it the Beijing Trio. So like his group M’Boom — it’s not the Max Roach — and I think on an earlier recording he wanted to focus on, was it “Hasaan”? Incredible pianist recording, I think it was in 1965 on Atlantic. But he had an original voice. And that’s one of the things that Max Roach really embraced about my — not really the way I perform on piano, but my thinking. So actually when I approached him about “SenseUs: The Rainbow Anthems,” and that was to reconceptualize the Star Spangled anthem — the national anthem — why does the national anthem have to be a song? Why can’t it be a poem? Why can’t the national anthem — why is it only one national anthem? Why can’t there be more anthems that speak to the majority of people in this country? And why is the “Star Spangled Banner,” which is a celebration of war, why is it that for most people, who can only sing an octave, eight pitches, why do we sing the national anthem which has twelve pitches?
